warmup.q: One copy of a program is restarting while another runs PUBLISH payments:status "p-981 approved", which sends a message on a channel named payments:status. One second later, the restarted copy starts listening on that channel. What does it receive?
options: The message: Redis keeps it until every listener has read it
The message, if it starts listening within the channel's retention time
Nothing: the message went to whoever was listening at that moment, and Redis kept no copy
An error that tells it a message was missed
warmup.why: Pub/sub stores nothing and keeps nothing for later. PUBLISH pushes the message to the connections listening at that instant and returns how many there were; then the message is gone. The Redis docs call this at-most-once: delivered once, if at all. The tempting second option borrows Kafka's retention, which pub/sub doesn't have. A stream, the second section's tool, keeps its entries, so a reader that comes back can carry on from the last one it saw.

sections.h: Pub/sub calls a message out to whoever is listening, then forgets it
sections.html:
Let's start with calling out. Redis is a program that keeps data in memory and answers many programs at once; the Caching track used it as a fast copy of a database. It also has two ways to pass messages between programs. The simpler one, pub/sub (publish and subscribe), keeps nothing at all. Meeting this track's ideas in a second product tests whether you learned the ideas, or only Kafka's names for them.

The café payments program has a job for it. When a payment's status changes, from waiting to approved, the customer's screen should change too. The program that draws those screens runs on 20 servers (computers that run a program for others), and each one must hear about the change. Asking Redis every 100 ms from 20 servers is 200 questions a second, for an event that happens a few times a minute per customer.

Pub/sub turns that around. A program sends SUBSCRIBE payments:status, and its connection to Redis switches into a mode where it only listens. Any other program can then run PUBLISH payments:status "p-981 approved". Redis pushes the message to every connection listening on that channel at that moment. It does so on the single loop that runs all its commands (Inside an in-memory store: how Redis executes commands). PUBLISH returns how many listeners it reached. A channel is only a name. It isn't stored, it takes no memory when nobody listens, and Redis's numbered databases all share it.

The catch is that Redis keeps no copy. A server might be restarting, its connection might have dropped for two seconds, or it might be too slow to read. Then the messages published in the meantime are gone for it, and nobody is told. That's Sam's coffee. The Redis docs say it plainly: pub/sub delivery is at-most-once, and a message the listener couldn't handle is "forever lost".

A slow listener is the quiet case. Redis holds its unread messages in an output buffer, memory set aside for each connection. By default it cuts off a pub/sub connection whose buffer passes 32 MB, or stays above 8 MB for 60 seconds. The program reconnects and subscribes again, and everything in between is lost.

So pub/sub fits messages whose loss nobody would notice, or that the receiver can rebuild. Think of "something changed, reload it", live dashboard updates, or hints that a cached copy is out of date (the client-side caching in Caching patterns and stampedes uses one). It doesn't fit "pay this shop for p-981". Redis Cluster spreads one Redis over several servers. There, SSUBSCRIBE and SPUBLISH (sharded pub/sub, Redis 7.0) keep each channel on one server, instead of copying every message to every server.

That sets up this lesson's picture. Pub/sub is a broadcast that keeps nothing, like a café calling out drinks. A stream is a log that keeps everything until you trim it, like orders written on a board. A consumer group on that stream remembers who took each order and whether it's done. Next, we'll write the messages down.

try.title: Publish to nobody
steps: Open two terminals in the labs folder, and start Redis if it isn't running: docker compose -f env/redis.yml up -d. In the first terminal, listen from redis-cli, Redis's command-line tool: docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli SUBSCRIBE payments:status.
In the second terminal (docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli), publish two messages and watch the first terminal.
Stop the listener with Ctrl-C, publish a third message, and ask Redis how many listeners the channel has. Then subscribe again. Does p-983 arrive?

code.title: the publisher's prompt
code.html:
PUBLISH payments:status "p-981 approved"
PUBLISH payments:status "p-982 declined"
# now press Ctrl-C in the subscriber's terminal
PUBLISH payments:status "p-983 approved"
PUBSUB NUMSUB payments:status

try.expect: The listener first prints 1) "subscribe", 2) "payments:status", 3) (integer) 1. Each of the first two PUBLISHes returns (integer) 1, and the listener prints 1) "message", 2) "payments:status" and the text. After Ctrl-C, the third PUBLISH returns (integer) 0, and PUBSUB NUMSUB shows 2) (integer) 0. Subscribing again shows only the confirmation: p-983 was never stored anywhere.

sections.h: A stream writes every message down: a log in one key
sections.html:
To keep messages, store them. A Redis stream is a key, a named value in Redis, that holds a log: a list you only ever add to at the end. Each entry is a small set of field-value pairs, like a form with labelled boxes, and gets an ID that Redis assigns:

XADD payments * payment p-981 amount 1250
"1794082605087-0"

The * asks Redis for the next ID. The part before the dash is the server's clock in milliseconds, and the part after it numbers the entries added in the same millisecond. IDs only grow: if the clock goes backwards, Redis keeps using the last time it saw. So an ID is a position in the log and a rough timestamp at once.

Reading doesn't remove anything. XRANGE payments - + returns every entry in order (- and + stand for the lowest and highest IDs), and XRANGE payments <id> + COUNT 100 pages forward from an ID. XREAD COUNT 100 STREAMS payments <last-id> returns the entries after the last ID you saw. With BLOCK 5000 it waits up to 5 seconds for new ones, so a reader doesn't have to keep asking. Each reader keeps its own position, the last ID it handled. After a reconnect it asks for everything after that ID and misses nothing, because the log is still there. In the café, that's an order board: Sam comes back, reads down from the last order he saw, and finds his flat white.

Any number of readers can follow the same stream, each from its own position. An audit job that checks the books reads from the first entry, and a live screen reads from $, which means "only entries added after this call". Every reader sees every entry. That's fan-out, one message to many readers, the job pub/sub did, now without losses.

A log that keeps everything grows until Redis runs out of memory, so you trim it. XADD payments MAXLEN ~ 100000 * ... keeps about the last 100,000 entries. The ~ lets Redis keep a few more than that, which makes trimming much cheaper than cutting to exactly 100,000. MINID ~ <id> trims by age instead, since IDs are times. Inside, a stream is a tree of small, tightly packed blocks (a radix tree of listpacks, from Core data types and their encodings). Each block holds up to 100 entries or 4 KB by default (stream-node-max-entries and stream-node-max-bytes).

Now hold it next to Kafka's log from The log: Kafka's one big idea. A stream is like one partition: one ordered log in one key on one server, or in one slot of a Redis Cluster, the share of keys that one server holds. To spread the load, you create several streams and send each key to one of them yourself. The ID does the offset's job, but it's a time and a counter rather than a plain count, so IDs leave gaps and tell you when an entry arrived.

The log lives in memory, not in files on disk, so it holds what fits in memory. At a few hundred bytes an entry, a million payments take a few hundred megabytes, where a Kafka broker keeps a week on disk. Trimming does the job of Kafka's retention, and both work in chunks: Kafka deletes whole segment files, and MAXLEN ~ removes whole blocks of the tree.

Durability, surviving a crash, is weaker too, as Persistence and replication in the Caching track showed. XADD answers from memory. The entry reaches disk only through snapshots (RDB) or the append-only file (AOF), and copies on other servers catch up a moment later. So a failover, when a copy takes over from a failed server, can lose entries Redis already confirmed. Kafka with acks=all answers only once its in-sync copies have the record (The cluster: KRaft, replicas and the ISR). Next, we'll share the stream out between workers.

try.title: Append, read, block and trim
steps: At a redis-cli prompt (docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli), start from an empty stream, add three payments and read them back three ways.
Trim the stream to exactly 2 entries (no ~), then read the first entry. Which payment is it now?
In a second terminal, run XREAD BLOCK 0 STREAMS payments $. It waits. Add one more payment in the first terminal and watch the second.

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.html:
DEL payments
XADD payments * payment p-981 amount 1250
XADD payments * payment p-982 amount 4000
XADD payments * payment p-983 amount 990
XLEN payments
XRANGE payments - + COUNT 1
XREAD COUNT 2 STREAMS payments 0
XTRIM payments MAXLEN 2
XRANGE payments - + COUNT 1
# second terminal: XREAD BLOCK 0 STREAMS payments $
XADD payments * payment p-984 amount 2500

try.expect: The first DEL prints (integer) 0, or 1 if an earlier run left the key behind. Each XADD prints an ID such as "1794082605087-0": the server's time in ms, then a sequence number. Yours differ, and they always grow. XLEN prints (integer) 3. XRANGE ... COUNT 1 returns p-981 with its fields, and XREAD ... 0 returns p-981 and p-982 under the stream's name. XTRIM prints (integer) 1, and the first entry is now p-982: trimming drops the oldest. The blocked XREAD in the second terminal returns the moment p-984 is added, with that entry's ID and fields.

sections.h: A consumer group shares the stream out and writes down every delivery
sections.html:
Paying shops is a different job from showing payments on a screen. Each night the company pays each shop what it took. Before that, workers settle each payment: they add it to the shop's payout, the amount the company owes that shop. (The code calls these workers settlers.) Three workers should share the stream, so that each payment goes to exactly one of them. And if a worker dies holding a payment, somebody has to know.

That's a consumer group. XGROUP CREATE payments settlers $ MKSTREAM creates a group named settlers that starts at the end of the stream ($; use 0 to start from the first entry). MKSTREAM also creates the stream if it doesn't exist yet. Each worker reads through the group under its own consumer name:

XREADGROUP GROUP settlers w1 COUNT 10 BLOCK 2000 STREAMS payments >

> means "entries never delivered to anyone in this group". Redis hands each new entry to one consumer only, so three workers split the stream between them. Redis creates a consumer the first time it sees its name.

Redis also writes down every delivery. When it hands an entry to w1, it adds the entry's ID to the group's pending entries list (PEL). With the ID go the consumer's name, the time of delivery and a delivery count. In the café, that's the order board with a barista's initials next to each order they've taken. The entry stays pending until w1 confirms it with XACK payments settlers <id>, an acknowledgement that says it's done. A worker that crashes after reading and before XACK leaves its entries in the PEL under its name. Nothing is lost; it's only stuck, and the next section unsticks it.

XPENDING payments settlers sums up the PEL: how many entries are pending, the lowest and highest ID, and how many each consumer holds. XPENDING payments settlers - + 10 lists them one by one, with owner, idle time in milliseconds and delivery count. A restarted worker reads its own pending entries first. XREADGROUP ... STREAMS payments 0 returns the entries already delivered to it and not acknowledged, and adds one to their delivery count. When that comes back empty, the worker switches to >.

This is at-least-once delivery: every entry is settled at least once, and now and then twice, when a worker settles it and crashes before its XACK. So the handler must be idempotent, which means safe to run twice. Give it an idempotency key, as in Consumers: the poll loop, offsets and delivery guarantees. With the payment id as the key, the second settlement finds the payment done and changes nothing.

Now compare the two kinds of consumer group, which share a name and little else. A Kafka group gives each partition to one member and saves one offset per partition. So order holds, and one stuck record holds back everything behind it (Failure handling: poison pills, retries and dead letters). A Redis group keeps one last-delivered ID for the whole stream plus a state for every delivered entry, and hands entries to whichever member asks. That's the queue from Queues and brokers, or a share group, built on a log. A slow entry doesn't hold back the ones after it, and the price is that entries finish in any order. Next, we'll see what happens to a dead worker's entries.

try.title: Split a stream between two workers
steps: At a redis-cli prompt (docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli), start clean, create the group and add four payments. Explicit IDs (1-1, 1-2, ...) make the commands easy to type; real programs use *.
Read two entries as w1 and two as w2, then try a third read as w2. Look at XPENDING before and after w2's XACK.
Play w1 restarting: it asks for its own pending entries with ID 0. Compare the delivery counts in the last XPENDING with the earlier one.

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.html:
DEL settle
XGROUP CREATE settle settlers $ MKSTREAM
XADD settle 1-1 payment p-1 amount 1250
XADD settle 1-2 payment p-2 amount 4000
XADD settle 1-3 payment p-3 amount 990
XADD settle 1-4 payment p-4 amount 310
XREADGROUP GROUP settlers w1 COUNT 2 STREAMS settle >
XREADGROUP GROUP settlers w2 COUNT 2 STREAMS settle >
XREADGROUP GROUP settlers w2 COUNT 2 STREAMS settle >
XPENDING settle settlers
XACK settle settlers 1-3 1-4
XPENDING settle settlers - + 10
XREADGROUP GROUP settlers w1 STREAMS settle 0
XPENDING settle settlers - + 10

try.expect: The first DEL prints (integer) 0, or 1 if an earlier run left the key behind. w1 gets 1-1 and 1-2, w2 gets 1-3 and 1-4, and w2's third read prints (nil): nothing new is left. The summary shows 1) (integer) 4, IDs "1-1" to "1-4", and 2 pending for each of w1 and w2. XACK prints (integer) 2. The list then shows only 1-1 and 1-2, owner "w1", idle a few ms (more if you typed slowly), delivery count (integer) 1. w1's read with 0 returns those same two entries, and afterwards their delivery count is (integer) 2 and their idle time is back near 0. Keep this stream: the last Try-it uses it.

sections.h: When a worker dies, another one claims its entries
sections.html:
w1 read three payments, and then the operating system killed it for using too much memory (it was OOM-killed: out of memory). Its three entries sit in the PEL under its name, and > won't give them to anyone else, because they were already delivered. Someone has to take them over. In the café, a barista went home with three orders still marked with their initials.

XCLAIM payments settlers w3 30000 <id> moves a pending entry to w3, but only if it has been idle for at least 30,000 ms. That idle check stops w3 from stealing an entry that w1, alive but slow, is still working on, because delivering or claiming an entry resets its idle time. XAUTOCLAIM (Redis 6.2) does the search for you. XAUTOCLAIM payments settlers w3 30000 0-0 COUNT 100 scans the PEL from the start and claims up to 100 entries idle for at least 30 seconds. It returns a cursor, the place to carry on from, plus the claimed entries. Call it again with the cursor until the cursor comes back as 0-0. Sometimes it finds an entry that was trimmed out of the stream in the meantime. Then it drops it from the PEL and reports its ID in a third list (Redis 7.0).

Each claim adds one to the entry's delivery count, and that count is how you find a poison message. That's an entry that makes every worker fail, such as a payment in a currency the settlement code doesn't accept. Without a limit, it's claimed, fails, waits 30 seconds and is claimed again, forever.

Redis counts the deliveries but never acts on the count, and no timer hands an entry back by itself. A share group, from Share groups and running Kafka in production, archives a record after 5 deliveries and frees it when its 30-second lock runs out. A Redis entry waits until some consumer claims it. Redis counts, but it never decides. Give every consumer group a recovery loop and a dead-letter rule. When the delivery count passes, say, 5, copy the entry to a dead-letter stream for a person to look at, and XACK it. The lab's DeadLetters does that in one MULTI/EXEC, Redis's way of running several commands as one block, so the entry can't end up in both places or in neither.

Pick the idle threshold from your slowest normal run. If settling one payment can take 20 seconds at the bank, a 5-second threshold makes two workers settle the same payment. If it's 10 minutes, a crash delays payments by 10 minutes.

In the demo, the claim right after the crash found nothing, because the entries had been idle for well under a second. 1.1 seconds later they had been idle past the 1,000 ms threshold, all three were claimed in one call, and their delivery count went from 1 to 2. Next, we'll see how the newest Redis releases shorten this code.

stepper.intro: Payments 1-1 to 1-5 in the stream payments, the group settlers, and three workers. Idle times are in milliseconds.

try.title: Crash a worker and recover its entries
steps: Run CrashRecoveryDemo or CrashRecoveryDemoKt from the labs folder (commands below). w1 reads three payments and never acknowledges them; w2 reads and acknowledges the other two.
Before you look, predict how many entries the first XAUTOCLAIM claims, right after the crash, with a 1,000 ms threshold.
Read the delivery counts before and after the claim. What would they be after a second crash and claim?

code.title: CrashRecoveryDemo.java
code.html: package sfz.msg.l12.demo; import redis.clients.jedis.RedisClient; import redis.clients.jedis.StreamEntryID; import redis.clients.jedis.params.XAddParams; import redis.clients.jedis.params.XAutoClaimParams; import redis.clients.jedis.params.XPendingParams; import redis.clients.jedis.params.XReadGroupParams; import redis.clients.jedis.resps.StreamEntry; import redis.clients.jedis.resps.StreamPendingEntry; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** Worker w1 reads three payments and dies before XACK. Worker w3 claims them once they have been idle for 1 s. */ public class CrashRecoveryDemo { static final String STREAM = "demo:l09:payments"; static final String GROUP = "settlers"; static List<StreamEntry> readNew(RedisClient redis, String consumer, int count) { List<Map.Entry<String, List<StreamEntry>>> reply = redis.xreadGroup(GROUP, consumer, XReadGroupParams.xReadGroupParams().count(count), Map.of(STREAM, StreamEntryID.XREADGROUP_UNDELIVERED_ENTRY)); return reply == null || reply.isEmpty() ? List.of() : reply.get(0).getValue(); } static void printPending(RedisClient redis) { List<StreamPendingEntry> pending = redis.xpending(STREAM, GROUP, XPendingParams.xPendingParams("-", "+", 10)); System.out.println(" XPENDING: " + pending.size() + " pending"); for (StreamPendingEntry p : pending) { System.out.printf(" %s owner=%s idle=%d ms deliveries=%d%n", redis.xrange(STREAM, p.getID(), p.getID()).get(0).getFields().get("payment"), p.getConsumerName(), p.getIdleTime(), p.getDeliveredTimes()); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (RedisClient redis = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build()) { redis.del(STREAM); redis.xgroupCreate(STREAM, GROUP, StreamEntryID.XGROUP_LAST_ENTRY, true); // XGROUP CREATE ... $ MKSTREAM for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { redis.xadd(STREAM, XAddParams.xAddParams(), Map.of("payment", "p-" + i, "amount", String.valueOf(1000 + i))); } List<StreamEntry> w1 = readNew(redis, "w1", 3); // w1 takes three... and its pod is killed List<StreamEntry> w2 = readNew(redis, "w2", 10); // w2 takes the rest and settles them for (StreamEntry e : w2) redis.xack(STREAM, GROUP, e.getID()); System.out.println("w1 read " + w1.size() + " and crashed; w2 read " + w2.size() + " and acknowledged them"); printPending(redis); var early = redis.xautoclaim(STREAM, GROUP, "w3", 1_000, new StreamEntryID(0, 0), XAutoClaimParams.xAutoClaimParams().count(100)); System.out.println("w3 XAUTOCLAIM min-idle 1000 ms, right away: claimed " + early.getValue().size()); Thread.sleep(1_100); var claimed = redis.xautoclaim(STREAM, GROUP, "w3", 1_000, new StreamEntryID(0, 0), XAutoClaimParams.xAutoClaimParams().count(100)); System.out.println("w3 XAUTOCLAIM min-idle 1000 ms, 1.1 s later: claimed " + claimed.getValue().size() + ", next cursor " + claimed.getKey()); printPending(redis); for (StreamEntry e : claimed.getValue()) redis.xack(STREAM, GROUP, e.getID()); // settle, then ack System.out.println("w3 acknowledged them. XPENDING total: " + redis.xpending(STREAM, GROUP).getTotal()); } } }

alt.title: CrashRecoveryDemo.kt
alt.html: package sfz.msg.l12.demo import redis.clients.jedis.RedisClient import redis.clients.jedis.StreamEntryID import redis.clients.jedis.params.XAddParams import redis.clients.jedis.params.XAutoClaimParams import redis.clients.jedis.params.XPendingParams import redis.clients.jedis.params.XReadGroupParams import redis.clients.jedis.resps.StreamEntry /** Worker w1 reads three payments and dies before XACK. Worker w3 claims them once they have been idle for 1 s. */ private const val STREAM = "demo:l09:payments" private const val GROUP = "settlers" private fun RedisClient.readNew(consumer: String, count: Int): List<StreamEntry> = xreadGroup(GROUP, consumer, XReadGroupParams.xReadGroupParams().count(count), mapOf(STREAM to StreamEntryID.XREADGROUP_UNDELIVERED_ENTRY))?.firstOrNull()?.value.orEmpty() private fun RedisClient.printPending() { val pending = xpending(STREAM, GROUP, XPendingParams.xPendingParams("-", "+", 10)) println(" XPENDING: ${pending.size} pending") for (p in pending) { val payment = xrange(STREAM, p.id, p.id).single().fields["payment"] println(" $payment owner=${p.consumerName} idle=${p.idleTime} ms deliveries=${p.deliveredTimes}") } } fun main() { RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build().use { redis -> redis.del(STREAM) redis.xgroupCreate(STREAM, GROUP, StreamEntryID.XGROUP_LAST_ENTRY, true) // XGROUP CREATE ... $ MKSTREAM (1..5).forEach { redis.xadd(STREAM, XAddParams.xAddParams(), mapOf("payment" to "p-$it", "amount" to "${1000 + it}")) } val w1 = redis.readNew("w1", 3) // w1 takes three... and its pod is killed val w2 = redis.readNew("w2", 10) // w2 takes the rest and settles them w2.forEach { redis.xack(STREAM, GROUP, it.id) } println("w1 read ${w1.size} and crashed; w2 read ${w2.size} and acknowledged them") redis.printPending() val early = redis.xautoclaim(STREAM, GROUP, "w3", 1_000, StreamEntryID(0, 0), XAutoClaimParams.xAutoClaimParams().count(100)) println("w3 XAUTOCLAIM min-idle 1000 ms, right away: claimed ${early.value.size}") Thread.sleep(1_100) val claimed = redis.xautoclaim(STREAM, GROUP, "w3", 1_000, StreamEntryID(0, 0), XAutoClaimParams.xAutoClaimParams().count(100)) println("w3 XAUTOCLAIM min-idle 1000 ms, 1.1 s later: claimed ${claimed.value.size}, next cursor ${claimed.key}") redis.printPending() claimed.value.forEach { redis.xack(STREAM, GROUP, it.id) } // settle, then ack println("w3 acknowledged them. XPENDING total: ${redis.xpending(STREAM, GROUP).total}") } }

try.expect: w1 read 3 and crashed; w2 read 2 and acknowledged them, then 3 pending: p-1 to p-3, owner=w1, idle a few ms to a few hundred (29 ms in the Java run, 437 ms in the Kotlin one) and deliveries=1. The first XAUTOCLAIM prints claimed 0: the entries weren't idle long enough. 1.1 s later it prints claimed 3, next cursor 0-0, and the list shows owner=w3, idle near 0 and deliveries=2. After the XACKs, XPENDING total: 0. Another crash and claim would make the count 3.

sections.h: Redis 8.2 to 8.8 move Streams toward a queue
sections.html:
Four releases between August 2025 and May 2026 added stream commands that shorten the code above. Each one moves Redis Streams a step closer to the queue from the first lesson of this track. Each needs that Redis version or newer, so write the version down wherever your team keeps its notes on running the system. The dates below are the releases on Redis's GitHub releases page; the lab runs 8.10.3.

XACKDEL and XDELEX (8.2, August 2025) delete entries as they're acknowledged. A plain XACK only clears the PEL and leaves the entry in the stream, which is the log's way. XACKDEL payments settlers IDS 1 <id> acknowledges the entry for this group and deletes it from the stream in one command, which is the queue's way. Its option decides what happens to other groups that still have the entry pending. KEEPREF, the default, leaves their pending records of it, DELREF removes them too, and ACKED deletes only entries that every group has acknowledged. XDELEX is XDEL, the command that deletes an entry, with the same options, and XADD and XTRIM got them as well.

That matters because by default, MAXLEN trimming removes old entries even if some group still has them pending. The PEL keeps the ID, and reading it returns the ID with nil, Redis's empty value, instead of fields. With ACKED, trimming takes only what every group is done with.

XREADGROUP ... CLAIM <min-idle> (8.4, November 2025) folds recovery into the normal read. XREADGROUP GROUP settlers w3 COUNT 10 CLAIM 30000 STREAMS payments > first returns pending entries idle for at least 30 seconds, then new entries. Entries handed back with XNACK (below) come first, then the longest idle. Each claimed entry comes with two extra values: milliseconds since its last delivery, and how many times it was delivered before. One loop now covers new work and a crashed worker's work.

XADD ... IDMP <producer-id> <idempotent-id> (8.6, February 2026) stops repeats on the writing side. A program that times out on XADD and tries again can add the same payment twice, and the group would settle both. With IDMP, Redis remembers each writer's recent ids and returns the original entry's ID instead of adding a second entry. On the lab server, it remembered the last 100 ids per writer for 100 seconds (XINFO STREAM shows idmp-maxsize and idmp-duration), and XCFGSET changes both. That window covers a retry, not a replay of yesterday's file.

IDMP is close to Kafka's idempotent producer from Producers II, with one difference. Kafka's producer numbers its own batches, while IDMP compares an id you supply, more like an idempotency key with a short memory.

XNACK (8.8, May 2026) lets a worker hand entries back on purpose, instead of waiting for them to be claimed. The entries lose their owner and can be claimed at once, whatever the idle threshold. Its mode says what happens to the delivery count. SILENT subtracts one, for a clean shutdown where the delivery shouldn't count. FAIL leaves it, for "I couldn't do this one, let someone else try". FATAL sets it to the maximum, which marks a poison message so that your dead-letter rule catches it at once. FAIL is the share group's RELEASE, and FATAL plays REJECT's part, through your own dead-letter rule.

So the two designs keep borrowing from each other, and the limit of the lighter one is clear. A stream lives in one key, in memory, on one server. It suits work that fits there, such as a queue of jobs inside one program. The history that many teams build on and read again belongs in Kafka.

try.title: Hand back, claim in the read, add twice, delete on ack
steps: Carry on at the same prompt, with the settle stream from the third Try-it: 1-1 and 1-2 are pending for w1.
Hand 1-1 back with XNACK ... FAIL and look at the PEL. Then add 1-5 and read as w3 with CLAIM 3600000: only entries idle for an hour qualify. Which entries come back, and in what order?
Add the same payment twice with the same IDMP writer and id, and count the entries.
Acknowledge and delete 1-1 and 1-5 in one command with XACKDEL, then look at the PEL and count the entries again. Are 1-3 and 1-4, which w2 acknowledged long ago, still in the stream?

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.html:
XNACK settle settlers FAIL IDS 1 1-1
XPENDING settle settlers - + 10
XADD settle 1-5 payment p-5 amount 700
XREADGROUP GROUP settlers w3 COUNT 10 CLAIM 3600000 STREAMS settle >
XPENDING settle settlers - + 10
XADD settle IDMP checkout-3 pay-6 * payment p-6 amount 2500
XADD settle IDMP checkout-3 pay-6 * payment p-6 amount 2500
XLEN settle
XACKDEL settle settlers IDS 2 1-1 1-5
XPENDING settle settlers - + 10
XLEN settle
XRANGE settle - +

try.expect: XNACK prints (integer) 1. The PEL now shows 1-1 with owner "", idle (integer) -1 and delivery count 2 (FAIL kept it), while 1-2 is still w1's. The CLAIM read returns 1-1 first, with two extra values: a huge "ms since last delivery" such as 1794082612818 (XNACK set its delivery time to 0, the start of 1970 as computers count time) and (integer) 2. Then comes the new 1-5, with 0 and 0. 1-2 isn't claimed: it hasn't been idle for an hour. The PEL then shows 1-1 and 1-5 owned by w3, 1-1 with 3 deliveries. Both IDMP XADDs print the same ID, such as "1794082612820-0", and XLEN prints (integer) 6: the retry added nothing. XACKDEL prints 1) (integer) 1 and 2) (integer) 1: both entries were acknowledged and deleted. The PEL now holds only 1-2, still w1's, and XLEN drops from 6 to (integer) 4. XRANGE still lists 1-2, 1-3, 1-4 and the IDMP entry. w2 acknowledged 1-3 and 1-4 with a plain XACK, which never deletes. That's the log's way, and XACKDEL is the queue's.

refs.title: XADD, with IDMP and trimming options

opening:
Picture a busy café that calls out each drink when it's ready: "Flat white for Sam!" At that moment Sam is washing his hands. Nobody calls it twice, and nobody writes it down. His coffee goes cold on the counter.

The café payments program sends messages like that. When a payment is approved, every screen that shows it must hear at once, and the quick way is to call it out to whoever is listening. Calling out is fast and cheap, so it's easy to use it for everything, including the messages that must never be missed.

In Share groups and running Kafka in production, a share group handed out single records from a log, with a lock on each. In this lesson, we'll meet Redis, a program that keeps its data in memory, and its two message tools: pub/sub, which calls out, and Streams, which writes everything down. Then we'll crash a worker halfway through a batch and still get every payment through. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a flat white called out once and never again, which is how pub/sub works. A stream writes each message down, and a consumer group remembers who took what. So a crashed worker's payments are claimed and finished by someone else.

With the lab's Redis running, after the Try-its, type XINFO GROUPS settle at the redis-cli prompt. Read the group's pending and lag, the two numbers that say whether its workers keep up.

That ends this track. Next, we start Stream processing. There our payments live in a database, and we'll ask how a second copy, such as a search screen, can follow every change without drifting apart.

compare.title: A settlement worker loop in Java and Kotlin

java.title: SettlementLoop.java
java.html: while (running) { List<Map.Entry<String, List<StreamEntry>>> batch = redis.xreadGroup("settlers", consumer, XReadGroupParams.xReadGroupParams().count(10).block(2_000), Map.of("payments", StreamEntryID.XREADGROUP_UNDELIVERED_ENTRY)); if (batch == null || batch.isEmpty()) continue; // BLOCK timed out: nothing new for (StreamEntry e : batch.get(0).getValue()) { try { settle(e.getFields()); // idempotent: keyed by the payment id redis.xack("payments", "settlers", e.getID()); } catch (Exception ex) { log.warn("left pending, a claim will retry it: " + e.getID(), ex); } } }

kotlin.title: SettlementLoop.kt
kotlin.html: while (running) { val batch = redis.xreadGroup("settlers", consumer, XReadGroupParams.xReadGroupParams().count(10).block(2_000), mapOf("payments" to StreamEntryID.XREADGROUP_UNDELIVERED_ENTRY)) ?.firstOrNull()?.value ?: continue // BLOCK timed out: nothing new for (e in batch) { runCatching { settle(e.fields) } // idempotent: keyed by the payment id .onSuccess { redis.xack("payments", "settlers", e.id) } .onFailure { log.warn("left pending, a claim will retry it: ${e.id}", it) } } }

compare.note: Both loops send the same commands: XREADGROUP with BLOCK, then one XACK per settled entry. A failure leaves the entry pending on purpose, and the recovery loop claims it later. Kotlin's safe calls (?.) and ?: continue turn the empty reply into one expression, and runCatching makes success and failure two named branches. One caution: runCatching also catches a coroutine's CancellationException, the signal that a coroutine should stop, so inside a coroutine rethrow it. Jedis, the Redis client library the labs use, borrows a pooled connection for the whole 2-second BLOCK, so size the pool for the number of workers. With Lettuce, another client library, give the loop a connection of its own.

worked.title: Replace the status pub/sub with a stream that every server reads

steps.say: The program that publishes now adds an entry instead of calling out. MAXLEN ~ 100000 keeps the stream bounded in the same command, and the reply is the new entry's ID.
steps.code: StreamEntryID id = redis.xadd("payments:status", XAddParams.xAddParams().maxLen(100_000).approximateTrimming(), Map.of("payment", "p-981", "status", "approved")); // XADD payments:status MAXLEN ~ 100000 * ...

alt.html: val id = redis.xadd("payments:status", XAddParams.xAddParams().maxLen(100_000).approximateTrimming(), mapOf("payment" to "p-981", "status" to "approved")) // XADD payments:status MAXLEN ~ 100000 * ...

steps.say: Each server reads the whole stream, so there's no group: every server sees every status change. The server keeps its position in lastId, starting at $, "only what arrives from now on", and blocks for up to 5 seconds instead of asking over and over.
steps.code: StreamEntryID lastId = StreamEntryID.XREAD_NEW_ENTRY; // "$" while (running) { List<Map.Entry<String, List<StreamEntry>>> reply = redis.xread( XReadParams.xReadParams().count(100).block(5_000), Map.of("payments:status", lastId)); if (reply == null || reply.isEmpty()) continue; // 5 s with nothing new for (StreamEntry e : reply.get(0).getValue()) { pushToBrowsers(e.getFields()); lastId = e.getID(); // our position in the log } }

alt.html: var lastId: StreamEntryID = StreamEntryID.XREAD_NEW_ENTRY // "$" while (running) { val entries = redis.xread(XReadParams.xReadParams().count(100).block(5_000), mapOf("payments:status" to lastId))?.firstOrNull()?.value ?: continue // 5 s with nothing new for (e in entries) { pushToBrowsers(e.fields) lastId = e.id // our position in the log } }

steps.say: Now a dropped connection costs nothing. When the connection comes back, the loop asks for everything after lastId, and the entries published while it was gone are still in the stream. With pub/sub, they were gone. A server that restarts begins again at $, which is right for a screen that only shows live updates.
Trim by age when time matters more than count. Stream IDs are milliseconds, so "one hour ago" is a number: now minus 3,600,000. MINID ~ with that number drops every entry older than an hour.

lab.title: A settlement worker that survives crashes, and a dead-letter sweeper
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. All 10 fail at first: six in SettlementWorkerTest and four in DeadLettersTest, against a Redis container the tests share. createGroup is already written; read it first.

In SettlementWorker.java, write processNew: one XREADGROUP with >, then settle and XACK each entry, leaving failures pending. Run ./gradlew :redis:test --tests 'sfz.msg.l12.SettlementWorkerTest': four tests pass.

Write recoverAbandoned with an XAUTOCLAIM loop that follows the cursor until it's 0-0. Read the test another worker recovers a crashed worker's entries ...: its first claim must find nothing, because the entries haven't been idle long enough yet.
In DeadLetters.kt, write sweep: XPENDING, then for each entry over the limit, XADD to the dead-letter stream and XACK, in one transaction. Run all 10 tests.
hints: redis.xreadGroup(...) returns null or an empty list when there's nothing new. Loop over every Map.Entry in the reply and over its getValue() list.
Put the settle-then-XACK step in one private method and call it from both processNew and recoverAbandoned, so a failure is handled the same way in both.
page.getKey() is the next cursor. Stop when it equals new StreamEntryID(0, 0): cursor.compareTo(start) == 0.
Kotlin sees getID(), getDeliveredTimes() and getFields() as id, deliveredTimes and fields. fields + mapOf("original-id" to p.id.toString(), ...) builds the copy.

drill.title: The recovery loop from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write recoverAbandoned(minIdleMillis) with Jedis, the Redis client library the lab uses: XAUTOCLAIM from cursor 0-0 in pages of 100, settle and XACK each claimed entry, and stop when the cursor comes back as 0-0. Then say why the idle threshold must be longer than your slowest settlement.

answer.html: int recoverAbandoned(long minIdleMillis) { StreamEntryID start = new StreamEntryID(0, 0); StreamEntryID cursor = start; int settled = 0; do { Map.Entry<StreamEntryID, List<StreamEntry>> page = redis.xautoclaim("payments", "settlers", consumer, minIdleMillis, cursor, XAutoClaimParams.xAutoClaimParams().count(100)); for (StreamEntry e : page.getValue()) { settle(e.getFields()); // idempotent by payment id redis.xack("payments", "settlers", e.getID()); settled++; } cursor = page.getKey(); // 0-0: the whole PEL was scanned } while (cursor.compareTo(start) != 0); return settled; } // a shorter threshold claims entries a live but slow worker is still settling: they get settled twice

alt.html: fun recoverAbandoned(minIdleMillis: Long): Int { val start = StreamEntryID(0, 0) var cursor = start var settled = 0 do { val page = redis.xautoclaim("payments", "settlers", consumer, minIdleMillis, cursor, XAutoClaimParams.xAutoClaimParams().count(100)) for (e in page.value) { settle(e.fields) // idempotent by payment id redis.xack("payments", "settlers", e.id) settled++ } cursor = page.key // 0-0: the whole PEL was scanned } while (cursor.compareTo(start) != 0) return settled } // a shorter threshold claims entries a live but slow worker is still settling: they get settled twice

recap: Pub/sub is at-most-once: PUBLISH reaches the listeners connected at that moment and stores nothing. Use it for signals a receiver can afford to miss.

A stream is a log in one key, in memory: like one partition, with <ms>-<seq> IDs where Kafka has offsets, and trimming (MAXLEN ~, MINID ~) where it has retention. Readers keep their own position and wait with XREAD BLOCK.

A consumer group gives each new entry (>) to one consumer and records it in the pending entries list until XACK. It's the queue again, built on a log, with at-least-once delivery, so handlers must be idempotent.
A crashed consumer's entries stay pending. XAUTOCLAIM with a minimum idle time hands them to a live one and adds one to their delivery count.

A rising delivery count marks a poison message, but Redis never acts on it: move it to a dead-letter stream and XACK it. Redis 8.2 to 8.8 added XACKDEL (8.2), XREADGROUP CLAIM (8.4), XADD IDMP (8.6) and XNACK (8.8).
The limit: a stream lives in memory, in one key on one server, and a failover can lose entries Redis already confirmed. For history that many teams read and replay, Kafka stays the record.

explain.prompt: The "payment settled" events are sent with PUBLISH today, and the ledger program subscribes. Explain to a teammate why that loses payments, and what changes when you move to a stream with a consumer group.
explain.answer: PUBLISH delivers to whoever is listening at that instant and stores nothing. Whenever the ledger program restarts, is updated or loses its connection for a second, the events published in that window are gone, and nothing tells anyone. A slow ledger can even be cut off by Redis when its output buffer grows past the pub/sub limit. With a stream, each event is an entry in a key. The ledger workers read through a consumer group: each new entry goes to one worker and is recorded in the pending entries list until that worker acknowledges it with XACK. If a worker dies before acknowledging, its entries stay pending, and a recovery loop with XAUTOCLAIM gives them to another worker once they've been idle long enough. So nothing is lost, but an entry can be handled twice, which means the ledger write must be idempotent, keyed by the payment id. We also need a dead-letter rule for entries whose delivery count keeps rising, a MAXLEN or MINID trim so the stream doesn't grow forever, and an alert on old pending entries.

deeper.html:
Measuring a group's backlog. XINFO GROUPS payments shows each group's last-delivered-id and how many entries are pending. Since Redis 7.0 it also shows entries-read and lag: how many entries were added after the group's last delivered one. Lag that keeps rising means the workers can't keep up; a pending count that keeps rising means they read but don't acknowledge.

Keyspace notifications. Redis can publish an event whenever a key changes or expires (notify-keyspace-events, off by default). It's built on pub/sub, so it inherits at-most-once delivery: a listener that was disconnected misses expirations for good. Don't build a job that must not fail on "tell me when this key expires".

Bounding a read. COUNT limits entries per stream. Redis 8.10 added MAXCOUNT and MAXSIZE to XREAD and XREADGROUP, to cap the total entries and bytes of one reply when a worker reads several streams at once.

An early IDMP caveat. Redis 8.6.0 shipped with one known limitation, which its release notes said the next patch would remove: avoid IDMP on a server with appendonly yes and the non-default aof-use-rdb-preamble no (two settings of the append-only file).

Choosing between them. For 50,000 settlement retries a day inside one program, a stream is simpler: one key, no partitions to size, an acknowledgement per entry. For the event history that several teams build on and replay, Kafka is the record. Valkey, an open-source program that split off from Redis in 2024, has streams too, but this course hasn't checked whether it has the Redis 8 commands above, so check its documentation before you rely on them.
